notes: VERSION CONFLICT: The Secretary of State compilation (rules.sos.ga.gov) was fetched for .01-.09(3), but its page cut off partway through .09(3)(a). That current text says an administrator must obtain a satisfactory fingerprint records check under the Criminal Background Checks rules. The Cornell LII mirror of .09 (original 2013 text) has no fingerprint requirement for administrators. DCH held a hearing on 6/16/2026 and posted a 'Final Adoption' notice dated 7/14/26. Before printing the manual, pull the full current SOS text of .09-.15 and the DCH notice, and reconcile every .09-.13 cite against it.

CORRECTION TO PRIOR RESEARCH: The research said supervisory visits are due every 122 days for all clients. The rule text says otherwise. Rule .10(2)(b)2 requires a visit at least every 92 days for clients receiving personal care tasks. Rule .10(2)(c)2 requires a visit at least every 122 days for companion/sitter-only clients. Use 92 days for any client who receives personal care.
The research said a plan of correction is due within 10 days. That is confirmed by .08(4) as 'ten days of the receipt of the written report'.

Rule 111-8-65 has NO rule on these topics: medication administration (aides may only remind and assist with self-administration, .03(k)), emergency or disaster preparedness, incident reporting to DCH, caregiver-to-client ratios, discharge notice periods, insurance minimums, and an aide registry. Policies on these topics rest on the cited definitions, on other law, or on internal standards. Each is labeled 'internal standard' in state_specifics.

Unverified and NOT used as citations: Georgia workers' compensation threshold, the $1M/$3M liability minimum, the GCHEXS fingerprint process for staff, the CMO versus fee-for-service payment route, waiver incident-reporting deadlines, and the HB 183 contractor limits (adoption status unknown). HFRD Private Home Care phone numbers conflict between DCH pages: (404) 657-9975 (HFRD Contacts page) and (404) 657-5700 (Private Home Care Program contact page). Confirm which to print in the service agreement.

citations.title: Legal Authority
citations.requirement: Rules are adopted under O.C.G.A. § 31-7-300 et seq.

citations.title: Definitions
citations.requirement: Defines: applicant/licensee by entity type (.03(b)); companion or sitter tasks (.03(c)); home management, where any employee with unlimited access to client funds must be bonded through the provider (.03(g)); medically frail or compromised client (.03(j)); medically related activities, including reminding clients to take medication and assisting with self-administration, but excluding professional services (.03(k)); owner as any person with 10% or greater interest (.03(l)); personal care tasks (.03(n)); private home care provider and services (.03(o)-(p)); transport and escort, which requires a client waiver of claims or reasonable efforts to confirm motor vehicle insurance when the employee drives a vehicle not owned by the client (.03(s)).

citations.title: Governing Body
citations.requirement: Each provider must have a governing body empowered and responsible to determine all policies and procedures and to ensure compliance with the rules.

citations.title: Licenses
citations.requirement: No operation without a license or provisional license (.05(1)). Owner must comply with Chapter 111-8-12 before a new license issues (.05(1)(b)). A provisional license may be issued to a new provider for a limited time or to an existing provider with an acceptable plan of improvement (.05(1)(c)). Administrator and employees must be qualified (.05(2)). Each location is separately licensed (.05(2)(a)). The license must be displayed (.05(2)(b)). It is not assignable or transferable. It must be returned on change of name, location, ownership or governing body. DCH must get 15 days' advance notice of a location change (.05(2)(c)).

citations.title: Applications
citations.requirement: Initial application on DCH forms, with application fee, Board-set license fee, owner records check application, and description of services and geographic area (.06(1)). Periodic renewal with a description of services and area (.06(2)). Fees are reasonable and may be refunded for good cause (.06(3)). Applications must be truthful. DCH may refuse a license for false statements (.06(4)).

citations.title: Exemptions
citations.requirement: Rules do not apply to an individual who personally provides services without agents, employees, contractors or financially interested referrals (.07(1)(a)), nor to licensed home health agencies (.07(1)(d)) or personal care home staff (.07(1)(e)). No Certificate of Need is required for a PHCP-only license (.07(2)).

citations.title: Inspections and Plans of Correction
citations.requirement: Periodic inspection, with possible exemption for accredited providers (.08(1)). Application or renewal is consent to entry during regular business hours, and DCH gets access to premises, records, staff and consenting clients (.08(2)). Staff must cooperate without unreasonable delay (.08(3)). An acceptable written plan of correction is due within ten days of receiving the written report. The provider may explain or dispute findings in the plan (.08(4)).

citations.title: Administration and Organization — Services Description
citations.requirement: Written policies and procedures must define the scope of services offered and the types of clients served. No service prohibited by the rules or other law may be provided.

citations.title: Administration and Organization — Service Agreements
citations.requirement: Do not offer services you cannot reasonably deliver. Written policies are required. All services are based on a written agreement with 10 required elements (.09(2)(a)1-10), including referral and contact dates, services, frequency, charges and billing, receipt of rights notice, the provider's phone number, the DCH phone number, authorization for client funds or vehicle use, and signatures. The agreement must be completed by the 2nd visit if on a different day than the 1st, or within 7 calendar days of first service, whichever is earlier (.09(2)(b)). Good-cause delay must be documented (.09(2)(b)1). Later changes are documented in the record as agreed by the client (.09(2)(b)2). The client may cancel at any time and pays only for services rendered. Only a reasonable travel and staff-time charge is allowed if the staff member has already arrived (.09(2)(c)).

citations.title: Administration and Organization — Administrator
citations.requirement: The governing body appoints an administrator with full authority and responsibility for operations. Qualifications: no credible evidence of abuse, neglect, exploitation or deprivation; participation in required orientation and training; no material false statements. The current SOS text of (3)(a)1 also requires a satisfactory fingerprint records check determination. See the notes on version conflict.

citations.title: Record keeping — Client Records
citations.requirement: A separate file per client containing: identifying information; current service agreement; current service plan; signed nursing notes if nursing is provided; documentation of personal care and companion/sitter tasks actually performed; supervisory visit findings; material reports and communications; physician contacts; date and source of referral.

citations.title: Retention and Confidentiality of Client Records
citations.requirement: Written policies must state who supervises records, who has custody, to whom and why records are released, and how long they are retained. Minimum retention is five years from the last service. Disclosure is allowed only to appropriate staff, the client, the responsible party, the client's physician or other provider, DCH, persons authorized in writing by the client, or by subpoena.

citations.title: Personnel Records
citations.requirement: A separate record per employee containing: identifying and emergency contact information; 5-year employment history; qualifications; satisfactory TB screening at hire and annually; date of employment; job description; orientation and training documentation; at least an annual performance evaluation; bonding documentation if the employee has unlimited access to client funds (a universal bond is acceptable).

citations.title: Reports of Complaints and Incidents
citations.requirement: Keep files of all complaints under .12(2). Keep incident reports and reports of unusual occurrences (e.g., falls, accidents, significant medication errors) for at least five years. Documentation must show actions taken to resolve complaints and address incidents.

citations.title: Staffing — General and Nursing Personnel
citations.requirement: Keep sufficient qualified staff for the service agreements. On an unexpected staff shortage, advise the client and refer to another provider if the client wishes. Staff must have a written competency evaluation by direct observation or demonstration. Hires must have no credible evidence of abuse or exploitation, must complete orientation and training, and must make no false qualification statements. Nursing personnel must hold a Georgia license.

citations.title: Personal Care Assistant (PCA) Qualifications
citations.requirement: A PCA must have one of: a nurse aide program under 42 CFR Part 483 Subpart D; a DCH-recognized nurse aide competency exam; a DCH-approved health care or personal care credential; or a 40-hour provider training program covering ambulation and transfer, personal care tasks, first aid and CPR, special conditions, home management, home safety and sanitation, infection control, medically related activities and vital signs, and nutrition. The 40-hour program must be directed by an RN or an equivalent professional. 20 hours must be completed before serving clients and the other 20 within six months of starting. No PCA may be assigned a task without completed training and a competency determination. No PCA may care for a client with special conditions without training and demonstrated competency.

citations.title: Companions or Sitters
citations.requirement: Companions or sitters may perform only companion or sitter tasks unless also qualified as a nurse or PCA. They must read, write, follow instructions and complete reports. They must be trained or competent in the needs of elderly, handicapped or convalescing persons, meal preparation, transport and escort, housekeeping and sanitation, home safety, handling medical emergencies, and infection control.

citations.title: Staff Training
citations.requirement: Orientation before working with clients must cover: written policies on scope of services and client types; client rights and complaints (.12); the employee's duties; reporting client progress and problems and handling medical emergencies and incidents; and the duty to report known exposure to TB or hepatitis. Each employee must receive at least 8 clock hours of training annually after the first year of employment, in subjects relating to their duties.

citations.title: Contracted Services
citations.requirement: Contractor arrangements must be in writing and detail the services. The provider must ensure the contractor follows the rules and is qualified. The services must be supervised under .10(2) by a supervisor of the licensed provider.

citations.title: Categories of Services
citations.requirement: Nursing services are delivered by an RN or LPN under a supervisor. Personal care tasks are performed by a qualified PCA (or nurse) per the service plan. Companion or sitter tasks are performed by a qualified companion or sitter per the service plan. PCAs, companions and sitters must report client needs, changes in condition and observed problems.

citations.title: Supervision of Services; Nursing Supervision
citations.requirement: Qualified staff must supervise all services. Each staff member must be evaluated in writing at least annually by direct observation or demonstration. No supervisor may knowingly permit an employee who has been exposed to or diagnosed with TB or hepatitis to serve clients until the employee is determined not to be contagious. A provider offering nursing must employ a fully licensed Georgia RN supervisor.

citations.title: Supervision of Personal Care Tasks
citations.requirement: Supervisors must be qualified by education, training and experience. A licensed RN or LPN must supervise personal care for medically frail or compromised clients. An RN must complete the initial service plan for those clients. A supervisory home visit to the client's residence is due at least every 92 days from the date of initial service, or sooner as the level of care requires. The visit assesses general condition and vital signs, progress, problems, client satisfaction and appropriateness of services, and is documented in the client file or plan.

citations.title: Supervision of Companion or Sitter Tasks
citations.requirement: A qualified supervisor (RN, LPN, the administrator or another assigned staff member) completes the service plan. A supervisory home visit is due at least every 122 days from initial service, or when a complaint raises a serious question about services. The visit assesses condition, progress, problems, satisfaction and appropriateness of services, is made in the residence, and is documented.

citations.title: On-call Representative for Medically Frail Clients
citations.requirement: When staff perform personal care for medically frail or compromised clients in their homes, a provider representative must be on call and able to reach a nurse supervisor by phone or other means to consult with staff on the clients' medical needs.

citations.title: Documentation of Home Care Services Provided
citations.requirement: Written policies must provide for documenting the services actually performed each day. The documentation goes into the client file under .09(4)(a).

citations.title: Quality Improvement Program
citations.requirement: Maintain documentation of an effective quality improvement program that continuously monitors program performance and client outcomes against standards of care and the rules. At minimum, document receipt and resolution of complaints, problems with care identified, and corrective actions.

citations.title: Service Plans
citations.requirement: Written policies are required. The plan is developed with the client, the responsible party, and the physician if nursing is provided. Content: functional limitations, services, times and frequency, duration, goals and objectives, and discharge plans. Where applicable it also covers diagnoses, medications and treatments, equipment, and diet. The service supervisor completes the plan within seven working days after services start. Nursing plans are reviewed and updated at least every 62 days. Other plans are reviewed at each supervisory visit and revised when the content items change.

citations.title: Client Rights, Responsibilities, and Complaints
citations.requirement: A written notice of rights and responsibilities must be given when the service agreement is completed. It covers 11 items (.12(2)(a)-(k)): participation in planning, being informed of changes, accepting or refusing services, charges, the supervisor's name and contact, complaint procedures and non-retaliation, confidentiality, respect for property and residence, DCH address and phone, a copy of the most recent inspection report on written request (after the plan of correction is filed, with a reasonable copying charge), and the client's duty to report changes in condition. Also required: oral or written complaint procedures with timely resolution (.12(3)), and giving the provider's phone number for information, questions and complaints (.12(4)).

citations.title: Enforcement and Penalties
citations.requirement: After notice and an opportunity for hearing, DCH may refuse, limit, restrict, suspend, revoke or refuse to renew a license, issue a public reprimand, or impose a fine.

citations.title: Rules and Regulations for Criminal Background Checks
citations.requirement: The owner must comply before a new PHCP license is issued (per .05(1)(b)). Which positions beyond the owner and administrator are covered was not verified; confirm with HFRD.

citations.title: In-Home Services
citations.requirement: CCSP in-home service providers must hold a current, valid DCH private home care license.

citations.title: Georgia Elderly and Disabled Waiver (CCSP/SOURCE)
citations.requirement: 1915(c) waiver approved 11/09/2022 to 11/08/2027. DCH handles reimbursement, enrollment and utilization review, and DAS runs day-to-day CCSP operations.

citations.cite: 21st Century Cures Act (2016) § 12006 — EVV; Georgia DCH EVV program
citations.title: Electronic Visit Verification
citations.requirement: EVV is required for Medicaid-financed personal care services. Georgia's system is Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+. Each visit records service type, recipient, provider, date, location and start/end times. Waiver billing: CCSP/SOURCE (IDs 590/930) T1019 with TF/UC; ICWP (660) and NOW/COMP (680/681) T2025.

citations.title: Reporting of need for protective services
citations.requirement: Persons with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult or elder person has been abused, neglected or exploited must report to the designated adult protection agency (DHS-DAS Adult Protective Services) and to an appropriate law enforcement agency or prosecutor. A staff member of a hospital, social agency, financial institution or similar facility must notify the person in charge, who reports or causes the report. Any other person may report. Good-faith reporters are immune (§ 30-5-4(c)). The statute's list of mandated reporters was seen only in part; the agency's policy treats every caregiver as a reporter.

citations.title: Third-party employers of home care workers
citations.requirement: Per the provided research: third-party employers (agencies) may not claim the companionship exemption from overtime. The 2026 status of this section was not confirmed, so verify before finalizing the overtime policy.

policies.title: Governing Body and Administrator Responsibilities
state_specifics: The governing body determines ALL policies and procedures and ensures compliance with Rule 111-8-65 (.04).

The licensee depends on entity type (.03(b)). A sole proprietor is the licensee. General partners are the licensee for a partnership. For an LLC, association or corporation, the entity is the licensee and its governing body authorizes the application and completes the statement of responsibility.

The governing body appoints an administrator with full authority and responsibility for operations (.09(3)). Administrator minimums: no credible evidence (court, jury, DCH investigation or other reliable evidence) of abuse, neglect, sexual assault, exploitation or deprivation; completes required orientation and training; no material false statements. Get a signed attestation at hire.
Current SOS text adds a satisfactory fingerprint records check determination for the administrator (.09(3)(a)1). Confirm against the 2026 compilation.
Owner = any person with 10% or greater ownership interest who exercises owner authority or operates the business (.03(l)). Owners must satisfy Chapter 111-8-12.

policies.title: Licensure, Service Area and Advertising Requirements
state_specifics: No operation without a DCH license or provisional license. A provisional license is for a new provider to demonstrate compliance in a reasonable but limited time, or for an existing provider with an acceptable plan of improvement (.05(1)(c)).

Each office location is separately licensed. The license is displayed at the licensed location. It cannot be assigned or transferred. Return it to DCH on change of name, location, ownership or governing body. Give DCH 15 days' advance written notice of a location change (.05(2)(a)-(c)).

The application and renewal each must describe the services offered and the geographic area served (.06(1)-(2)). Keep the county list current. Renewal is 'periodic' with a Board-set fee, and the interval is not stated in the rule, so calendar the exact date HFRD gives.
Applications must be truthful. False statements can result in refusal to issue or renew (.06(4)).

Advertising limits (internal standard anchored to the license): advertise only services in the application and the policy under .09(1). Do not advertise nursing unless an RN supervisor is employed (.10(2)(a)). State that the agency is a DCH-licensed private home care provider.
No Certificate of Need for PHCP-only licensure (.07(2)). A separate license is required for home health agency or personal care home operation.
Exemption check: the individual-direct exemption (.07(1)(a)) does not apply to any business using employees, contractors or financially-interested referrals.

policies.title: Policy Review and Document Control
state_specifics: Rule 111-8-65 requires written, implemented policies on: scope of services and client types (.09(1)); service agreements (.09(2)(a)); client record maintenance and security (.09(4)(b)); daily service documentation (.10(3)); service planning (.11(1)); client rights and complaints (.12(1)).
The governing body approves each policy (.04). Version-date every policy and keep a signed approval log.

Review cycle: internal standard of at least annually and on any rule change. Re-check the SOS compilation and DCH public notices every six months, because Rule 111-8-65 had a 2026 revision (public hearing 6/16/2026; final adoption notice 7/14/26).
Keep prior versions available to show surveyors what policy applied on a given date. Document staff training on each revision.

policies.title: Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement
state_specifics: Rule requires documentation of an effective quality improvement program that continuously monitors both program performance and client outcomes against standards of care and the rules (.10(4)).
Minimum content: record receipt and resolution of client complaints, problems with care identified, and corrective actions taken.

Suggested audit items (internal standard): supervisory visits on time (92 or 122 days), service agreements signed within the deadline, service plans completed within 7 working days, TB screens current, training hours and annual evaluations current, incident and complaint trends.
Run an annual self-audit against Rule 111-8-65 and report results to the governing body.

policies.title: Corporate Compliance, Fraud and Billing Integrity
state_specifics: Applies in full to Medicaid waiver billing (CCSP/SOURCE, ICWP, NOW/COMP). For private-pay-only agencies, keep the fraud and truthfulness rules as internal standards.
Applications and renewals to DCH must be truthful (.06(4)).

Bill only for visits actually delivered and documented. Waiver claims must be supported by EVV and by the service plan. A claim for a service not performed, or for unqualified staff, is a false claim.
No payments for referrals. Note that .03(o)(3) treats financially-interested referral arrangements as private home care provider activity requiring licensure.
Waiver in-home providers must hold a current valid DCH PHCP license (HCBS 5300 Manual § 208). Loss of the license ends waiver eligibility.
Designate a compliance officer and a hotline for staff concerns. Prohibit retaliation.

policies.title: Services Description and Types of Clients Served
state_specifics: Written policy must define the scope of private home care services offered and the types of clients served (.09(1)). The orientation covers this policy for every employee (.09(6)(a)1).

Choose the categories offered: personal care tasks (bathing, toileting, grooming, shaving, dental care, dressing, eating, plus nutrition, home management, housekeeping, ambulation and transfer, and medically related activities including vital signs only with those tasks); companion or sitter tasks (transport and escort, meal preparation and serving, household tasks essential to cleanliness and safety); and nursing (RN or LPN only).

Excluded from 'private home care services' (.03(p)(4)): physical, speech and occupational therapy, medical nutrition therapy, medical social services, home health aide services of a licensed home health agency, and proxy caregiver services hired by the patient.
The 'residence' must be a home (own, friend's or relative's, or a personal care home). Hospitals, nursing homes, hospices and similar licensed facilities are not residences (.03(q)).
Do not accept a client whose needs exceed your scope or your trained staff's competencies (.09(2) lead-in; .09(5)(c)2).

policies.title: DCH Inspections, Plans of Correction and Enforcement
state_specifics: DCH inspects periodically with no fixed interval. It may exempt a provider that is certified or accredited by a DCH-recognized body (the provider must submit its most recent report). DCH may inspect whenever it decides necessary (.08(1)).

Application or renewal constitutes consent to entry during regular business hours. DCH gets reasonable and meaningful access to premises, records relevant to licensure, all staff, and consenting clients (.08(2)). Staff must cooperate and provide documents without unreasonable delay (.08(3)).
'Inspection' includes surveys, monitoring visits and complaint investigations (.03(i)).

Plan of correction: due within TEN days of RECEIPT of the written report. It must state what will be done and when for each violation. The provider may explain or dispute findings in the plan (.08(4)). Designate one person to log receipt of the report the day it arrives.
Clients may request the most recent completed inspection report. The provider may hold it until the plan of correction is filed and may charge reasonable copy costs (.12(2)(j)).
Enforcement: after notice and hearing, DCH can reprimand, limit, restrict, suspend, fine, refuse to renew or revoke the license (.13(3)).

policies.title: Contracted Services and Worker Classification
state_specifics: Any arrangement with independent contractors, individuals or agents must be written and detail the services (.09(7)).
The provider must assure the contractor follows the rules and is qualified, and a supervisor of the licensed provider must supervise the contractor's services under .10(2).
Contractors are supervised and trained to the same standard as employees, including the 92-day or 122-day supervisory visits.

Definition limit: under .03(o)(2), independent contractors count in the definition only if they are health care professionals licensed under Title 43. DCH proposed (HB 183, adoption status unverified) to limit contractors to licensed Title 43 professionals. Default policy: aides are W-2 employees.
Referring a caregiver where the referrer has an ownership or financial interest in delivering the service makes the referrer a provider requiring a license (.03(o)(3)).

policies.title: Client Rights and Responsibilities
state_specifics: Give each client or responsible party a written notice of rights and responsibilities when the service agreement is completed (.12(2)). The service agreement must acknowledge receipt (.09(2)(a)6).

The notice must include all of (.12(2)(a)-(k)): (a) informed about and participate in the plan of service; (b) promptly and fully informed of plan changes; (c) accept or refuse services; (d) be informed of charges; (e) name, business phone and address of the supervisor and how to contact; (f) complaint procedures, right to complain without fear of discrimination or retaliation, and investigation within a reasonable time, with name, address and phone of the complaint handler; (g) confidentiality of the record; (h) respect for property and residence; (i) written notice of DCH address and phone, with the explanation that DCH licenses the provider and investigates complaints that appear to violate licensing rules; (j) copy of the most recent licensure inspection report on written request; (k) notice that the client and responsible party must tell the provider about changes in condition or events affecting service needs.
'Responsible party' = anyone authorized in writing by the client or appointed by a court, including a family member of an impaired client unable to authorize (.03(r)).
Waiver clients: also provide the program's own rights and appeal information (CCSP/SOURCE, ICWP, NOW/COMP). Confirm the contents with DAS or DBHDD provider manuals.

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
state_specifics: Accept complaints orally or in writing from clients 'and others' and resolve them in a timely manner (.12(3)).
Provide every client and responsible party the provider's specific phone number for information, questions and complaints (.12(4)). The same number goes into the service agreement (.09(2)(a)7).
Name the complaint handler with business address and phone (.12(2)(f)). No retaliation or discrimination for complaining.
The rule sets no resolution deadline. Internal standard: acknowledge within 2 business days and resolve or give a written status in 14 days.

A complaint that raises a serious question about the services triggers an extra supervisory home visit on a companion/sitter case (.10(2)(c)2). Apply the same practice to personal care clients as an internal standard.
Maintain a complaint file showing every complaint and the actions taken to resolve it (.09(4)(d)). Retain at least five years. Feed trends into the QI program (.10(4)).
Tell clients they may call DCH HFRD Complaint Intake toll free at (800) 878-6442 or file online with HFRD if the provider does not resolve a licensing concern (.09(2)(a)8).

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
federal: 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164 (HIPAA Privacy, Security, Breach Notification), applicable if the agency bills Medicaid or other payers electronically
state_specifics: The provider must keep client records confidential (.09(4)(b)1). Employees may disclose record information only to: appropriate provider staff, the client, the responsible party, the client's physician or other health care provider, DCH, others authorized in writing by the client, or under subpoena (.09(4)(b)2).
Written policy must say who supervises records, who has custody, to whom and for what purposes records are released, and how long they are retained (.09(4)(b)).
Confidentiality is a stated client right (.12(2)(g)). Cover it in orientation.
DCH access to records under .08(2) is a permitted disclosure; log the access.
HIPAA: issue a Notice of Privacy Practices and obtain acknowledgment from covered clients. Appoint a privacy officer. Apply the minimum necessary rule. Keep breach notification procedures.

policies.title: Client Property, Gifts and Financial Exploitation Prevention
state_specifics: The client has the right to have property and residence treated with respect (.12(2)(h)).

An employee with unlimited access to a client's personal funds for home management must be bonded through the provider (.03(g)). Bonding documentation goes in the personnel record; a universal bond is acceptable (.09(4)(c)9).

The service agreement must contain the client's or responsible party's written authorization for access to personal funds when home management includes bill paying or shopping with client funds (.09(2)(a)9).
Prohibit employees from borrowing from clients, accepting gifts above a nominal value, becoming beneficiaries, or using client credit cards or accounts (internal standard).
Suspected financial exploitation is a reportable event under O.C.G.A. § 30-5-4. See SAF-01 for APS reporting.
Require receipts and a running balance log for any client money handled.

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
federal: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 USC 2000d)
Americans with Disabilities Act (42 USC 12101 et seq.)
Section 1557 of the ACA (45 CFR Part 92), applicable if the agency receives federal financial assistance such as Medicaid
Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (29 USC 794), same applicability
state_specifics: Clients have the right to complain without fear of discrimination or retaliation (.12(2)(f)).

Rule 111-8-65 contains no language-access provision. Federal law governs. Provide interpreters or translated vital documents (rights notice, service agreement, complaint procedure) at no cost for clients with limited English proficiency, and auxiliary aids for clients with disabilities.
Do not refuse services on a protected basis. Reasonable-accommodation requests go to the administrator.
Waiver clients: confirm any program-specific requirements with DAS or DBHDD.

policies.title: Service Agreement, Rates and Billing Disclosure
state_specifics: Every service must be based on a written service agreement with the client or responsible party (.09(2)(a)).

Required contents: (1) initial contact date; (2) referral date (the date a specific request was received); (3) services needed as stated by the client; (4) services to be provided, with frequency and duration; (5) charges and billing and payment mechanisms; (6) acknowledgment of the rights and responsibilities notice; (7) provider's phone for information, questions and complaints; (8) DCH phone number for unresolved licensing concerns; (9) authorization for access to client funds and for use of the client's motor vehicle, if applicable; (10) signatures and dates. If the client refuses to sign, note the refusal and an explanation.

Deadline for new clients: by the second visit if it falls on a different day from the first, or within seven calendar days after services start, whichever is earlier (.09(2)(b)). Document good cause if not completed (.09(2)(b)1).
Changes in service, frequency, duration or charges: note the specific change in the record and that the client or responsible party agreed before the change takes effect (.09(2)(b)2).

Cancellation: the client may cancel at any time and pays only for services rendered before notice. Only a reasonable charge for travel and staff time may be assessed if the staff member has already arrived (.09(2)(c)). Do not use minimum-hour or non-cancellable terms.
Do not offer services you cannot reasonably expect to deliver (.09(2)). Print the DCH number confirmed by HFRD (complaint intake (800) 878-6442).

policies.title: Client Access to Licensure Inspection Reports
state_specifics: On written request, give the client the most recent completed licensure inspection report (.12(2)(j)).
The provider need not release a report until it has had the opportunity to file its written plan of correction (ten-day window under .08(4)).
The provider may charge reasonable photocopying fees.
Log the request date and the release date.

policies.title: Scope of Services — What Caregivers May and May Not Do
state_specifics: Personal care assistants (PCAs) may perform personal care tasks and companion or sitter tasks. They may NOT provide nursing services unless licensed (.09(5)(c)).
Companions or sitters perform only companion or sitter tasks unless also qualified as PCA or nurse (.09(5)(d)1).
Nursing services are limited to Georgia-licensed RNs and LPNs (.03(p)(1); .09(5)(b)).

Vital signs may be taken only in conjunction with personal care tasks (.03(n)). 'Medically related activities' include observing and reporting changes, arranging doctor trips, picking up prescriptions, accompanying clients to appointments, recording intake and output, reminding clients to take medications and assisting with self-administration. They never include professional services regulated under practice acts (.03(k)).

No employee is assigned a task for which training is incomplete and competency has not been determined. No PCA is assigned to a client with special conditions without training and competency for those conditions (.09(5)(c)2).

Provide a 'may do / may not do' task list for each worker type. Examples of prohibited tasks: injections, wound care or sterile procedures, insulin or medication administration, catheter care and tube feeding (unless licensed nurse), or physical, speech or occupational therapy (excluded by .03(p)(4)).
Do not provide services prohibited by the rules or other laws (.09(1)).

policies.title: Client Intake, Eligibility and Assessment
state_specifics: Record the date of initial contact and the date of referral (the date a specific request for services was received) on the service agreement (.09(2)(a)1-2). Record the date and source of referral in the client file (.09(4)(a)9).
Do not offer services the provider cannot reasonably expect to deliver under the rules (.09(2)). Match requested hours, tasks and client needs to qualified staff before accepting.
At intake, screen whether the client is 'medically frail or medically compromised' (.03(j)). If so, an RN must complete the initial service plan and a nurse must supervise (.10(2)(b)).
Identify the responsible party and obtain written authorization (.03(r)).

Waiver clients: eligibility is determined by the program entry point, not the provider. CCSP/SOURCE goes through the Area Agencies on Aging and DAS. NOW/COMP goes through DBHDD. ICWP goes through its program office. Do not collect fees contrary to the waiver plan of care.
Payer intake: verify authorization, service units and EVV set-up before the first visit.

policies.title: Service Plan and Plan Updates
state_specifics: A written plan of service is established with the client, the responsible party and, when nursing services are provided and the client has a personal physician, the physician (.11(1)).

Required content: functional limitations, types of service, expected times and frequency in the residence, expected duration, goals and objectives, and discharge plans. When applicable: diagnoses, medications and treatments, equipment needs, and diet and nutrition (.11(1)(a)-(b)).
Deadline: the service supervisor completes the plan within SEVEN WORKING DAYS after services are first provided in the residence (.11(2)).

Review and update: nursing service plans at least every 62 days; other plans at each supervisory visit (every 92 days for personal care and every 122 days for companion/sitter-only), and revise whenever the content items change (.11(2)).

Who may complete: the appropriate supervisor per .10(2)(a)-(c), in coordination with the staff who will provide services. For medically frail or compromised clients an RN completes the initial plan. An LPN may make later revisions, which the RN reviews timely (.10(2)(b)1).
Keep the current plan in the client file (.09(4)(a)3).

policies.title: Supervision of Caregivers and Supervisory Visits
state_specifics: Supervisory home visit: at least every 92 DAYS for clients receiving personal care tasks, counted from the date of initial service in the residence, or sooner as the level of care requires (.10(2)(b)2). At least every 122 DAYS for companion/sitter-only clients (.10(2)(c)2), or sooner when a complaint raises a serious question about services.

The 92-day visit includes an assessment of general condition AND vital signs, progress, problems, client satisfaction, and appropriateness of the level of services. The 122-day visit covers the same elements except vital signs. Visits must be in the residence and documented in the client file or service plan (.10(2)(b)2, (c)2; .09(4)(a)6).
Each staff member must be evaluated in writing at least annually by direct observation or demonstration of the tasks they perform (.10(2)).

Supervisor qualifications: for personal care, qualified by education, training and experience. An RN or LPN supervises personal care for medically frail or compromised clients (LPN reports to an RN). For companion/sitter tasks, an RN, LPN, the administrator or another assigned staff member may supervise (.10(2)(b)-(c)).
On-call: when staff provide personal care to medically frail or compromised clients, a provider representative must be on call and able to contact a nurse supervisor (.10(2)(d)).
Supervisors may not knowingly permit an employee exposed to or diagnosed with TB or hepatitis to serve clients until determined not contagious (.10(2)).
Track the next-due date for every client in the scheduling system. Alert at 14 days before due (internal standard).

policies.title: Medication Assistance and Self-Administration Support (Medically Related Activities)
state_specifics: Rule 111-8-65 has no medication administration rule. Non-nurse caregivers may only REMIND clients to take medication and ASSIST WITH SELF-ADMINISTRATION as medically related activities. They may not perform activities that are professional services under practice and licensing statutes (.03(k)).
Caregivers do not select, measure, draw up, inject, or give medications for the client. Nurses may administer within their scope under the service plan (.10(1)(a)).
Picking up prescriptions and accompanying clients to appointments are permitted medically related activities (.03(k)).
The service plan lists medications where applicable (.11(1)(b)).

A significant medication error is an 'unusual occurrence' that must be documented and kept at least five years (.09(4)(d)). Report it to the supervisor the same day (internal standard) and see SAF-02.
Train every caregiver on this scope limit at orientation and in annual in-service.

policies.title: Scheduling, Missed Visits and Continuity of Care
state_specifics: Keep sufficient qualified staff to deliver the services in the service agreements (.09(5)).

If the provider becomes aware it cannot deliver services because of an unexpected staff shortage, it must advise the client and refer the client to another provider if the client wishes (.09(5)). Notify the client promptly (internal standard: same day).
Employees must follow the service plan (.10(1)). Document every visit and each task actually performed (.10(3); .09(4)(a)5).

Missed-visit procedure (internal standard): caregiver calls the office at once if unable to attend. The scheduler finds a qualified replacement. The client is called. Log every missed or late visit and the reason, and review the log in QI.
Assign only workers qualified for the tasks and any special conditions (.09(5)(c)2).
Waiver clients: report missed visits as required by the payer or case manager. Confirm the timeline in the program manual.

policies.title: Electronic Visit Verification and Timekeeping
state_specifics: EVV is required for Medicaid-financed personal care. Georgia's state system is Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+ (MCG+).
Each visit must capture at minimum: service type, recipient, provider, service date, location, and start and end times.

DCH EVV page: EVV is required on claims for dates of service on or after 2026-09-14 for Home Health/HHCS claims. Verify applicability to your waiver codes with DCH. Claims are submitted through GAMMIS.
Georgia EVV Customer Support: (833) 483-5587 (the previous number was retired 1/16/2026).
Private-pay visits: use an internal time and task record, because the rule requires daily documentation of services actually performed (.10(3)).
Manual edits: require a reason code, supervisor approval and an audit trail. Review edits weekly.
Time records also support FLSA payroll. See PER-06.

policies.title: Change in Client Condition and Emergencies in the Home
state_specifics: PCAs and companions must report on client needs, changes in condition and any observed problems affecting the client (.10(1)(b)-(c)).
Orientation must cover reporting client progress and problems to supervisors and the procedures for handling medical emergencies or other incidents affecting delivery of services (.09(6)(a)3).
Companion/sitter competency must include handling medical emergencies in the home (.09(5)(d)2(ii)). First aid and CPR are part of the 40-hour PCA program (.09(5)(c)1(iv)(III)).
For medically frail or compromised clients, an on-call provider representative must be reachable and able to reach a nurse supervisor by phone (.10(2)(d)).
Clients and responsible parties must tell the provider about changes in condition (.12(2)(k)).
Internal standard: call 911 first for life-threatening events, then notify the supervisor, then the family or responsible party and physician as authorized. Document in the client record.
A significant change triggers a service plan revision (.11(2)).

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Discontinuation of Services
state_specifics: The client may cancel the service agreement at any time. The client is charged only for services rendered before the provider is notified (.09(2)(c)).
The service plan must include discharge plans (.11(1)(a)).
If the provider cannot deliver services because of an unexpected staff shortage, it must refer the client to another provider on request (.09(5)).

Rule 111-8-65 sets no provider-initiated discharge notice period. Internal standard: written notice of at least 14 days with referral options, except where safety of the client or staff requires immediate action.
Document the reason, notice, referral and last date of service in the record. The five-year retention clock starts at the last service date (.09(4)(b)1).
Waiver clients: notify the case manager or support coordinator before discontinuing, as the program requires.

policies.title: Coordination with Medicaid Programs and Payers
federal: 42 CFR 441.301(b) (plan of care requirements, as applicable)
state_specifics: Georgia waiver programs: Elderly and Disabled Waiver (CCSP/SOURCE, administered with DAS and the Area Agencies on Aging), ICWP, and NOW/COMP (DBHDD).
In-home service providers must hold a current valid DCH private home care license (HCBS 5300 Manual § 208).
DCH handles provider reimbursement, enrollment and utilization review. DAS runs day-to-day CCSP operations (CMS Waiver 0112.R08.00, approved 11/09/2022-11/08/2027).
Provide only services authorized in the participant's plan of care. Coordinate with the case manager or support coordinator on changes, hospitalizations and discharges.
Payer rate and unit details must come from written DCH or program sources.
Whether personal support is paid fee-for-service or through a CMO was not confirmed. Confirm in writing with DCH.

policies.title: Documentation of Daily Services Provided
state_specifics: Written policy must provide for documenting the services actually performed for each client each day. The documentation is incorporated into the client file (.10(3)).
The client file must hold documentation of personal care and companion/sitter tasks actually performed (.09(4)(a)5).
Nursing: clinical and progress notes signed and dated by the staff providing care (.09(4)(a)4).
Caregiver notes are completed at the end of each visit. Late entries are labeled and dated (internal standard).
Never pre-chart tasks. Never document tasks not performed.

policies.title: Staff Shortage Notification and Client Referral
state_specifics: Do not accept new clients unless staffing can meet the service agreements (.09(2); .09(5)).
On an unexpected staff shortage, advise the client and refer the client to another provider if the client wishes (.09(5)).
Keep a current list of alternate licensed providers (check GaMap2Care for licensed PHCPs).
Document the notice and the client's choice in the record.

policies.title: Medically Frail or Medically Compromised Clients and Nurse Consultation
state_specifics: Definition: a client whose health status, as determined by appropriate staff under accepted standards of practice, is likely to change or has changed because of disease, injury, disability or advanced age (.03(j)).
An RN or LPN supervises personal care for these clients. An LPN reports to an RN, who remains responsible for the service plan (.10(2)(b)).
An RN completes the initial service plan. Subsequent revisions may be made by a supervising LPN and are reviewed in a timely manner by the RN (.10(2)(b)1).

An on-call provider representative must be reachable and able to contact a nurse supervisor by phone or other means to consult with employees or subcontractors about the client's medical needs (.10(2)(d)).
Staff assigned to clients with special conditions must be trained and shown competent for those conditions (.09(5)(c)2).

policies.title: Nursing Services (Optional Module — Only If Offered)
state_specifics: Offer nursing only if the agency employs a fully licensed Georgia RN supervisor (.10(2)(a)).

Nursing services must be provided by an RN or LPN in accordance with nursing practice laws and the service plan, and include regular assessment of needs, participation in the service plan, services as planned, and reporting problems and progress to supervisors or the client's physician (.10(1)(a)).
Nurses must be Georgia-licensed (.09(5)(b)). Verify licenses at hire and at renewal.
The plan is developed with the client's personal physician if there is one (.11(1)). Nursing plans are reviewed at least every 62 days (.11(2)).
Clinical and progress notes are signed and dated (.09(4)(a)4).
If nursing is not offered, delete this policy and do not advertise nursing.

policies.title: Home Management, Bill Paying and Client Funds
state_specifics: Home management = activities normally performed by a homemaker for essential home services, such as meal planning, shopping and bill paying (.03(g)).
Any employee authorized unlimited access to a client's personal funds must be bonded through the provider (.03(g)). Keep bonding evidence in personnel records (.09(4)(c)9).
The service agreement needs written authorization from the client or responsible party for access to personal funds when services include bill paying or shopping with client funds (.09(2)(a)9).
If aides will not handle cash, state that in the agreement and policy.
Internal standard: receipts, balance logs, and dual signature for amounts above a set limit. Report discrepancies to the administrator the same day.

policies.title: Waiver Billing Codes and Claims Integrity
state_specifics: CCSP/SOURCE (waiver IDs 590/930): personal support bills under T1019 with TF or UC modifiers. T1019 is a 15-minute unit and is not for services identified as home health aide or CNA.
ICWP (660): T2025 with U5 plus TF or TG. NOW and COMP (680/681): community living supports under T2025 with U4 or U5.
Claims go through GAMMIS and must match EVV records.
Per-unit rates: no official rate was retrieved. Use written DCH sources only.
Reconcile EVV, timesheets and claims before submission. Correct and refund overpayments.

policies.title: HCBS Settings Requirements and Person-Centered Service Delivery (Waiver Clients)
state_specifics: Applies to clients served under the 1915(c) waivers (CCSP/SOURCE, ICWP, NOW/COMP).
Respect the participant's choice, privacy, dignity and control over daily activities and visitors, consistent with the plan of care.
Right to accept or refuse services and to be informed of plan changes (.12(2)(b)-(c)) supports the person-centered requirement.
Follow the participant's plan of care from the case manager or support coordinator. Do not restrict rights without a documented, plan-based justification.
Confirm program-specific requirements in the DAS and DBHDD provider manuals.

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
state_specifics: O.C.G.A. § 30-5-4: a person with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult or elder person has been abused (other than by accident), neglected or exploited must report to the designated adult protection agency AND to an appropriate law enforcement agency or prosecutor. The agency's policy treats every employee and contractor as a reporter.

Staff of a social agency or similar facility must notify the person in charge, who or whose designee reports or causes the report (§ 30-5-4(a)(1)(C)). Staff may also report directly (any person may report).

Georgia APS (DHS Division of Aging Services) intake: 1-866-552-4464, press 3, weekdays during business hours, or the online report form. Call 911 for emergencies. For persons in long-term care facilities, a different process applies.
A written report must follow the initial report. Secondary sources say within 24 hours. Verify the deadline in the statute before printing it.
Good-faith reporters are immune from civil and criminal liability (§ 30-5-4(c)). No retaliation.

Screen out workers with credible evidence of abuse, neglect, exploitation or deprivation at hire. Obtain the statement at application (.09(3)(a)1; .09(5)(a)1). Train on abuse reporting at orientation (.09(6)(a)3).
Document each report, the agencies notified and the outcome in the incident file (kept at least five years, .09(4)(d)).

policies.title: Incident Reporting
state_specifics: Keep on file for at least five years all incident reports and reports of unusual occurrences (e.g., falls, accidents, significant medication errors) that affect client health, safety and welfare. Documentation must show what actions the provider took (.09(4)(d)).

Rule 111-8-65 sets no deadline for reporting incidents to DCH. Internal standard: caregiver reports to the supervisor immediately; written incident report within 24 hours; administrator review within 2 business days.
Orientation covers handling of incidents affecting service delivery (.09(6)(a)3).
Notify the client's responsible party and, as applicable, physician and waiver case manager.
Trend incidents in the QI program (.10(4)).
Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation goes to APS and law enforcement. See SAF-01.

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
federal: 29 CFR 1910.1030 (Bloodborne Pathogens), where employees have occupational exposure
state_specifics: The 40-hour PCA program must cover infection control in the home and home safety and sanitation (.09(5)(c)1(iv)(VI)-(VII)). Companion/sitter competency includes infection control (.09(5)(d)2(ii)).
Orientation requires employees to report known exposure to tuberculosis and hepatitis to the employer (.09(6)(a)4).
Supervisors may not knowingly permit an employee who has been exposed to or diagnosed with TB or hepatitis to serve clients until determined not contagious (.10(2)).
TB screening documentation at hire and annually is a personnel record requirement (.09(4)(c)4).
Provide gloves and PPE. Standard precautions (hand hygiene, glove use, safe sharps and waste handling) are internal standards.
Use annual in-service time (8 clock hours) to refresh infection control.

policies.title: Client Emergency and Disaster Plans
federal: 42 CFR 441.301(c) (waiver plan of care risk planning, where applicable)
state_specifics: Rule 111-8-65 has no emergency preparedness or disaster plan requirement for PHCPs. This policy is an internal standard and good practice. Confirm waiver-specific requirements with DAS and DBHDD.

Anchored requirements: orientation covers handling medical emergencies and incidents (.09(6)(a)3). Companion/sitter competency includes handling medical emergencies in the home (.09(5)(d)2(ii)). An on-call representative is required for medically frail clients (.10(2)(d)).
Build a risk-tiered client list at intake: oxygen or power-dependent equipment, mobility limits, cognitive impairment, no caregiver backup.
Plan for severe weather, power outages and evacuation. Priority outreach goes first to medically frail clients.
Keep an after-hours number and an agency continuity plan covering staffing, records access and communications.
Test the plan at least annually.

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
state_specifics: Rule 111-8-65 has no workplace violence provision. Anchor: home safety is in the 40-hour PCA curriculum (.09(5)(c)1(iv)(VI)) and annual training is required on subjects related to duties (.09(6)(b)).
Pre-visit safety screening at intake (weapons, aggression, pets, hazards, unsafe neighborhood). Caregivers may leave an unsafe situation and must call the supervisor.
Safe lifting and transfer technique training (ambulation and transfer is a mandatory 40-hour topic, .09(5)(c)1(iv)(I)).
Report all injuries and assaults the same day. Workers' compensation coverage: confirm the Georgia threshold with a broker (not verified here).
No retaliation for refusing unsafe work.

policies.title: Transporting Clients
state_specifics: Transport and escort services = accompanying or providing or arranging transportation to places outside the residence (appointments, shopping, recreation, social activities) (.03(s)).

If the vehicle is NOT owned by the client and is driven by an employee, the provider must EITHER obtain the client's signed waiver of claims for damages from operation of the vehicle OR make reasonable efforts to ensure current motor vehicle insurance with medical coverage for the client (.03(s)). Keep the waiver or proof in the client file.
The service agreement must include approval for use of the client's motor vehicle if the client's vehicle will be used (.09(2)(a)9).
Companion/sitter competency includes transportation and escort services (.09(5)(d)2(ii)).
Internal standard: valid license, driving record check, proof of insurance, seat-belt use, no unsafe transfers, and mileage log. Add hired and non-owned auto coverage.

policies.title: Employee Exposure to TB, Hepatitis and Bloodborne Pathogens — Work Restrictions
state_specifics: Employees must report known exposure to TB or hepatitis to the employer (.09(6)(a)4).

No supervisor may knowingly allow an exposed or diagnosed employee to serve clients until it is determined the employee is not contagious (.10(2)). The determination comes from a health care provider; document it.
TB screening test is required upon employment and annually (.09(4)(c)4).
OSHA applies if employees have reasonably anticipated occupational exposure: written exposure control plan, hepatitis B vaccine offer, post-exposure evaluation and follow-up, sharps injury log.
Keep exposure records in a confidential medical file, separate from the personnel file.

policies.title: Waiver Critical Incident Reporting
state_specifics: Applies to clients served under the CCSP/SOURCE, ICWP and NOW/COMP waivers.
Specific waiver critical-incident categories and deadlines were NOT verified. Obtain them from the DAS HCBS manual and the DBHDD provider manual and insert them here before use.
All incidents are still documented and retained at least five years (.09(4)(d)).
Notify the case manager or support coordinator of serious events (injury, hospitalization, abuse, neglect, exploitation, death, missing person).

policies.title: Caregiver Qualifications and Credentials (PCA, Companion/Sitter, Nurse)
federal: 42 CFR Part 483 Subpart D (nurse aide training and competency programs, referenced by .09(5)(c)1(i))
state_specifics: Georgia has no separate state registry or certification for PHCP aides. Each PCA must satisfy one route (.09(5)(c)1): (i) nurse aide training and competency program under 42 CFR Part 483 Subpart D, (ii) DCH-recognized nurse aide competency exam, (iii) DCH-recognized health care or personal care credentialing program, or (iv) the provider's 40-hour training program.

Provider 40-hour program: topics (I)-(IX) include ambulation and transfer, personal care tasks, first aid and CPR, special conditions, home management, home safety and sanitation, infection control, vital signs and medically related activities, and nutrition. It is directed by an RN or equivalent. 20 hours before serving clients and 20 within six months of starting (.09(5)(c)1(iv), 2).
Companion/sitter: able to read and write, follow instructions and complete reports; trained or competent in the (.09(5)(d)2) topics.
Nurses: Georgia licensure (.09(5)(b)). Verify with the licensing board at hire.
Minimums for all hires: no credible evidence of abuse or exploitation, completes orientation and training, no false statements (.09(5)(a)1-3).
Obtain proof of credentials in the personnel record (.09(4)(c)3).

policies.title: Background Checks and Employee Registries
federal: 42 USC 1320a-7 and 42 CFR Part 1001 (OIG exclusion), for Medicaid providers
42 CFR 483.156 (nurse aide registry, where a CNA credential is used)
state_specifics: Owner: must comply with the Criminal Background Checks rules (Chapter 111-8-12) before a new license issues (.05(1)(b)); the application includes an owner records check (.06(1)).
Administrator: satisfactory fingerprint records check determination in the current SOS text of .09(3)(a)1. Verify.

Employees: obtain a written or oral statement at application that the person has never been shown by credible evidence to have abused, neglected, sexually assaulted, exploited or deprived any person (.09(5)(a)1). Whether fingerprint checks are required for non-owner staff under Chapter 111-8-12 must be confirmed with HFRD.
DCH may require additional verification of qualifications of the administrator and employees at any time (.05(2)).

Internal standard: check the OIG List of Excluded Individuals and Entities (LEIE), the Georgia Medicaid exclusion list, the sex offender registry, and the Georgia Nurse Aide Registry (for CNA credentials) at hire and monthly for Medicaid-billing staff.
Do not assign anyone to client contact until checks clear.

policies.title: Orientation, Competency Evaluation and Annual Training
state_specifics: Before working with clients, every employee providing services must be oriented (.09(6)). Orientation includes: the provider's written policies on scope of services and client types; client rights and complaints (.12); assigned duties; reporting client progress and problems and handling medical emergencies and incidents; and the duty to report known exposure to TB or hepatitis (.09(6)(a)1-4).

PCA: 40-hour program, 20 hours before client contact and 20 within six months of the date training began. RN or equivalent directs it. No assignment to any task until training is complete and competency is determined (.09(5)(c)2).
Companion/sitter: competency in the (.09(5)(d)2(ii)) areas.
Annual in-service: minimum 8 clock hours per employee annually after the first year of employment, on subjects related to the employee's duties (.09(6)(b)).
Competency: written evaluation by a supervisor by direct observation or demonstration of all required tasks (.09(5)(a); .10(2)). Evaluate at least annually.
Document orientation and training in the personnel record (.09(4)(c)7). Keep rosters, dates, hours, topics, trainer credentials and test results.

policies.title: Employee Health and TB Screening
state_specifics: Documentation of a satisfactory TB screening test upon employment and annually thereafter must be in each personnel record (.09(4)(c)4).
Rule does not specify the test type. Use an approved method (skin test or blood test) per health department or occupational-health guidance and record the date and result.
Employees must report known exposure to TB and hepatitis (.09(6)(a)4).
Employees exposed to or diagnosed with TB or hepatitis are removed from client contact until determined not contagious (.10(2)).
Keep medical documents confidential and separate from general personnel content except the TB documentation required in the file.

policies.title: Personnel Records
state_specifics: Keep a separate written record for each employee containing (.09(4)(c)): (1) name, address, phone, emergency contacts; (2) five-year employment history (or complete if shorter); (3) records of qualifications; (4) satisfactory TB screening at hire and annually; (5) date of employment; (6) job description or duties; (7) orientation and training documentation; (8) at least an annual performance evaluation; (9) bonding documentation if the employee has unlimited access to client funds (a universal bond may be documented once).
Also keep: statement on abuse/neglect history, background check results, credential proof, and the competency evaluations (.09(5)(a)).
The rule gives no personnel record retention period. Internal standard: at least five years after separation. FLSA payroll records are kept at least three years (29 CFR 516.5).
Make records available to DCH on inspection (.08(2)(a)).

policies.title: Wage, Hour and Overtime Compliance
state_specifics: Georgia's state minimum wage statute is $5.15, so the federal minimum of $7.25 applies to most employers.

Per the provided research, agencies as third-party employers cannot use the companionship exemption for overtime (29 CFR 552.109(a)). The 2026 status of this section was not confirmed; verify with the U.S. DOL before finalizing.
Pay overtime at 1.5 times the regular rate over 40 hours in a workweek, unless an exemption clearly applies.
Pay for travel between clients during the workday and for required training and orientation time (including the 20 pre-assignment hours and 8 annual in-service hours).
Keep accurate time records. Use EVV time as one source and reconcile.
Schedule to avoid unplanned overtime. Employees must not work off the clock.
Register with the Georgia DOL for unemployment insurance and confirm workers' compensation obligations with a broker.

policies.title: Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries
state_specifics: Respect client property and residence (.12(2)(h)).
Maintain confidentiality of client information. Disclose only as .09(4)(b)2 permits.
Orientation covers the provider's policies and employee duties (.09(6)(a)). Use it to train on boundaries.

Internal standard prohibitions: personal relationships with clients, social media posts about clients, loans or gifts, accepting transport or money from clients, working while impaired, bringing others to the client's home, or using client phones or vehicles for personal use.
Violations lead to discipline up to termination. Suspected abuse or exploitation is reported per SAF-01.

policies.title: Administrator and Supervisor Qualifications and Designation
state_specifics: Governing body appoints the administrator with full authority and responsibility (.09(3)). In an owner-operated agency, the owner may fill the role.
Personal care supervisors must be determined qualified by education, training and experience (.10(2)(b)). The rule sets no credential or years-of-experience figure.
An RN or LPN must supervise personal care for medically frail or compromised clients. An RN must supervise nursing services and be fully licensed in Georgia (.10(2)(a)-(b)).
Companion/sitter supervision: RN, LPN, the administrator, or another staff member assigned responsibility (.10(2)(c)).
Write job descriptions and keep them in the personnel record (.09(4)(c)6). Document the supervisor determination.

policies.title: Annual Performance Evaluation and Competency Observation
state_specifics: Each employee providing services must be evaluated in writing at least annually by their supervisor, through direct observation or demonstration of the job tasks they must perform (.10(2)).
Personnel record must contain documentation of at least an annual performance evaluation (.09(4)(c)8).
Competency must be determined for ALL required job tasks (.09(5)(a)).
Supervisors observe in the client's home. Document tasks observed and result. Retrain and re-evaluate on any gap.

policies.title: Client Records and Retention
federal: 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2) and 164.530(j) (HIPAA documentation retention, six years, for policies and related documentation)
state_specifics: One separate file per client containing: identifying information (name, address, phone, responsible party); current service agreement; current service plan; signed and dated nursing notes if nursing is provided; documentation of personal care and companion/sitter tasks actually performed; supervisory visit findings (unless in the plan); material reports and communications; physicians' names, addresses and phones; date and source of referral (.09(4)(a)1-9).
Retain client records at least FIVE YEARS from the date of last service (.09(4)(b)1).
Written policy must state who supervises records, who has custody, to whom records may be released and why, and how long they are kept (.09(4)(b)).
Store records securely with access controls and backups. Keep a destruction log after the retention period.
Waiver or payer record retention may be longer; apply the longer period. Confirm in the Medicaid provider agreement.

policies.title: Required Reports and Notices to the State
state_specifics: Rule 111-8-65 contains no routine periodic report to DCH. The required notices and submissions are:
Renewal application with a description of services offered and geographic area served, plus the Board-set renewal fee, on the date DCH sets (.06(2)).
Notice to DCH 15 days BEFORE any change of location (.05(2)(c)).
Return the license to DCH on change of name, location, ownership or governing body (.05(2)(c)).
Written plan of correction within ten days of receipt of an inspection report (.08(4)).
Accreditation documentation to DCH if seeking inspection exemption (.08(1)(a)).
Adult abuse, neglect or exploitation: report to APS (1-866-552-4464, press 3) and law enforcement (O.C.G.A. § 30-5-4).
Medicaid: EVV data and GAMMIS claims. Waiver case manager notifications.
DCH Private Home Care Program phone numbers vary across DCH pages: (404) 657-9975 and (404) 657-5700. Confirm before use.

policies.title: Complaint and Incident Files
state_specifics: Keep files of all documentation of complaints submitted under .12(2) (.09(4)(d)).
Keep incident reports and reports of unusual occurrences (falls, accidents, significant medication errors) for at least five years (.09(4)(d)).
Each file must show what actions the provider took to resolve the complaint or address the incident (.09(4)(d)).
Use a numbered log with date received, source, summary, investigator, findings, action and closure date.
Feed log summaries into the quarterly QI review (.10(4)).

policies.title: Release of Information, Subpoenas and Record Access
state_specifics: Employees may disclose record information only to: appropriate provider staff, the client, the responsible party, the client's physician or other health care provider, DCH, others authorized in writing by the client, or by subpoena (.09(4)(b)2).
DCH is entitled to reasonable and meaningful access to records relevant to licensure (.08(2)(a)). Staff must provide documents without unreasonable delay (.08(3)).
Obtain a written, signed, dated authorization for other releases. Log every disclosure.
Subpoena: route to the administrator, who confirms validity and seeks legal advice as needed.
Client access requests: respond within 30 days (HIPAA standard) where HIPAA applies.
